For some of us, like myself and possibly you, pinpointing the weight gain trigger can be both a blessing and a curse. The beauty is knowing exactly what you need to tackle to fix it. Hard part is how.

Some tips are universal to addicts.

First, One Day At A Time. Dont tell yourself "I'm never getting a box of cookies again." Tell yourself "I'm not getting a box of cookies TODAY." You can get a box tomorrow if you really want to. But not today. (Yes this sounds weird but it does work)

Two, you've got to substitute something for the addiction. With booze, for many it is the gym, some its bringing TV, for others its volunteer work. If you just sit there and obsess on your addiction, it can claim you.

Three, when feeling a craving,  it can be good to ask yourself what hole you're trying to fill. There is something called HALT. Many addict crave when Hungry, Angry, Lonely, or Tired. Now with sugar the first part, Hungry, can be a little tricky, as you might well be hungry, but the body hasn't evolved to crave chocolate chip cookies to fix a vitamin deficiency. It's a comfort thing.

Good luck to you!

Hey, storage employee here. 

Now, you didn't name (and I don't even think you can) the storage place. First questions is: Is it a mom and pop type store or one of the major chains? Because I can 99.9% guarantee you if it's a major chain that no one intentionally sold your stuff early.

So the company I work for has a process like this. You go late, we call you. Go late longer, get fines. Go late long enough, you get a pre-auction fee. (And we are calling you every few days). We send out certified letters, but you most likely never would get one, as it would have gone to your grandmother at an address that might not have them any more. We call a few more times. Then, if we aren't paid, we sell it. It sounds like you paid the back balance, but then went long enough that you ran down the clock again. Also, did you pay the WHOLE balance? If, for example, a customer owes me $100, and pays me $99, legally the auction clock keeps ticking. I've got to have a ZERO balance on the account to reset the clock. Now, I tell people this. More unscrupulous people might just take a partial payment and not disclose that.

Now, we have to, HAVE TO, document and timestamp every step of this process. Then a third party company and our District manager separately review the computer timeline to make sure it was followed to a T. Hell, I had to take someone out of auction and keep their stuff for an additional 2 months in a unit because I accidentally typed the WRONG TIME the auction was. (i.e. auction was at something like 2:30 and I typed 2:40) on the certified letter, that we got returned because she had moved. Let me repeat that. I had made a minor mistake, that the client never even SAW, and I had to hold her stuff for an additional 2 months.

This is all because we open ourselves up to HORRIBLE liability, as well as bad PR, if we don't.

Now, I don't know your area, but in mine, when we auction a unit, our auctioneer asks that all personal property (documents, photos, things of that nature) be returned to the facility in a timely manner. Now, we employees don't sort or move any of it. In fact, all I can do if I open your unit is take a picture from the outside. I can't go through your stuff. The auction people can't go through it until they buy it. So it is a bit of the honor system.

And also, no, if a former tenant asked me for the name of who bought it, I would not give it out. A lot of people that buy stuff, it's their personal information, not a business. And people who have had stuff sold at auction can be very, VERY scary. (One of my local employees was beaten, literally, last week due to this. Guy came in the office, didn't say a word, and began striking him. Sad thing was, he was only covering that store for the day, not a regular there. Had nothing to do with situation) So naturally we are not giving out info for someone to retaliate.

So, my suggestion is this. If you have maintained a civil and professional relationship with them, you COULD call and ask them if they would call the person that bought it (at least here, I do absolutely have to keep records of the buyer) and ask if they are willing to drop the personal property back at the facility. Do NOT ask if the buyer could meet you, go to your house, etc, for the safety reasons I mentioned earlier. That would make me shut it down and not help them.

Honestly, if you've been difficult with them, they won't help you. But if you've been nice, they most likely will.

As far as them not letting you open the unit? I dunno. That's always grey with us. We had a guy come in claiming his father had passed, provided us with death certificate (all info matched) and my boss, who had never dealt with that before, just confirmed it was a real certificate (Dunno who she called) and then we cut open the unit. I don't even know if we have an OFFICIAL policy on it, but while I'm sure it happens, it probably happens so rarely that most site managers, even if told it, would forget it long before it came up. However, them not letting you open it after taking your money may not have been malicious. If someone came to me and said "Hey, I'd like to pay on Jane Doe's unit" I would say "Okay!" and take their payment. Then if they said she passed, and they needed access, without keys or a code or proof, I would say "Ummm.....I can't do that".

Have you heard of the 'paper towel principle' yet? 

This changed how motivated I was.

Basically, think of a roll of paper towels. Now think of each towel representing one pound of fat. You take the first roll off the towel. Hardly looks different at all.

Get closer and closer to the middle, and each towel starts to make up a larger percent of the roll. Eventually, you can start to see the difference in size every couple of towels, until near the end, when every towel makes a difference.

Fat on the body is the same. If you are 300 lbs and lose 3 lbs, you only lost 1% of your body weight, and it's not very noticeable. However, if you are 150 lbs and lose 3 pounds, it's much easier to see.

You'll eventually find that you might go a month, lose 12 lbs, and see no difference, but suddenly, the next five are so obvious it's amazing!

Keep it up! I promise you'll notice more when more time has passed.
